steps.title: Number of classes
steps.body: $f(3)$ can be 1, 2 or 3, and each value is taken by some function, so there are **3** equivalence classes.

steps.title: Size of each class

cse-1996-b-57.approach: Prove $P(k)$: "$f_{3k}$ is even" by induction on $k$, using the recurrence twice to write $f_{3k+3}$ in terms of $f_{3k}$ and an even term.

steps.title: Base case
steps.body: $f_3=f_2+f_1=1+1=2$, which is even, so $P(1)$ holds.

steps.title: Inductive step
steps.body: Assume $f_{3k}$ is even. $2f_{3k+1}$ is even, and the sum of two even numbers is even, so $f_{3k+3}$ is even. Hence $P(k)\Rightarrow P(k+1)$, and by induction $f_3,f_6,f_9,\ldots$ are all even.

answer.value: Base: $f_3=2$ is even. Step: $f_{3k+3}=f_{3k+2}+f_{3k+1}=2f_{3k+1}+f_{3k}$, so if $f_{3k}$ is even then $f_{3k+3}$ is even. Hence every third term $f_{3k}$ is even.

pitfalls: The question asks for an induction proof about parity, not a closed form such as Binet's formula.

cse-1996-b-59.approach: A and B are nullable, C is not. Replace $S\to ABAC$ by every version with some nullable symbols dropped, delete the ε-rules, then remove the unit rule $S\to C$ that appears.

steps.title: Nullable symbols
steps.body: $A\to\varepsilon$ and $B\to\varepsilon$, so A and B are nullable. C and S are not (C must derive d).

steps.title: Expand $S	o ABAC$
steps.body:
Drop any subset of the three nullable positions $A_1,B,A_2$:
- none: $ABAC$
- $A_1$: $BAC$; $B$: $AAC$; $A_2$: $ABC$
- $A_1,B$ or $B,A_2$: $AC$; $A_1,A_2$: $BC$
- all three: $C$

Then $A\to aA\mid a$, $B\to bB\mid b$.

steps.title: Remove the unit production
steps.body: $S\to C$ is a unit production; replace it by C's right side: $S\to d$.

steps.body:
$$\begin{aligned}S&\to ABAC\mid BAC\mid AAC\mid ABC\mid AC\mid BC\mid d\\A&\to aA\mid a\\B&\to bB\mid b\\C&\to d\end{aligned}$$
$\varepsilon\notin L(G)$ (every string ends in d), so no $S\to\varepsilon$ is needed.

Dropping $A_1,B$ and dropping $B,A_2$ both give $AC$ — list it once.

cse-1996-b-60.approach: Concatenation: ε-move from every final state of $M_1$ to the start of $M_2$ and make $M_1$'s finals non-final. Star: add ε-moves from $M_2$'s final states back to $M_1$'s start. Because $\varepsilon\in L_1L_2$ already, no new start state is needed.
cse-1996-b-60.given:
| Machine | States | Language |
|---|---|---|
| $M_1$ | A (start, final), B; A↔B on 0 and 1 | even-length strings over {0,1} |
| $M_2$ | C (start, final), D (final), E (dead) | $a^*b^*$ |

steps.title: Part (a): $L_1L_2$
steps.body:
Add $A\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}C$ (A is $M_1$'s only final state). Start state: A. Make A **non-final**; final states: C and D. B and E unchanged.

Any accepting path reads an $M_1$ string ending in A (even length), takes ε to C, and then reads an $a^*b^*$ word ending in C or D.

steps.title: Part (b): $(L_1L_2)^*$
steps.body: To the machine of (a), add $C\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}A$ and $D\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}A$. Start A, finals C and D (A stays non-final).

steps.title: Why it is correct
steps.body:
- An accepting path splits at the ε-moves into blocks: (path A→A in $M_1$) ε (path C→C/D in $M_2$) ε back to A … so it spells a word of $(L_1L_2)^+$.
- Every word of $(L_1L_2)^+$ has such a path.
- $\varepsilon$: $A\xrightarrow{\varepsilon}C$ with C final, so ε is accepted. Since $\varepsilon\in L_1L_2$, $(L_1L_2)^+=(L_1L_2)^*$.
- A is never made final, so the usual trap (start state with incoming edges made final) does not occur: B→A edges cannot end a string in an accepting state.

answer.value: (a) Add ε: A→C; start A; A becomes non-final; final states C and D. (b) Additionally add ε: C→A and D→A (finals still C and D); ε is accepted through A→C, so the machine accepts $(L_1L_2)^*$.

pitfalls: Keeping A final in (a) happens to be harmless here (ε ∈ L₂, so L₁ ⊆ L₁L₂), but the general construction makes the finals of $M_1$ non-final.
Do not add ε from E — it is not a final state.

cse-1996-b-62.approach: The array is a Young tableau: rows and columns increase, so the minimum is $A[1][1]$. Insertion from the top-left corner is a "sift-down": while x is bigger than a right or lower neighbour, move the smaller neighbour up/left into the hole and follow it.

steps.title: Part (a)
steps.body: Every element is larger than its left and upper neighbours, so following them back always reaches $A[1][1]$: the smallest item is at $i=1$, $j=1$.

steps.title: Loop condition (line 2)
steps.body: Keep moving while x is out of order with a neighbour: x > A[i+1][j] **or** x > A[i][j+1].

steps.title: Which neighbour moves (lines 3, 7)
steps.body:
Move the **smaller** neighbour into the hole so it stays smaller than the other one:
- line 3: if A[i+1][j] < A[i][j+1] then move down (lines 4–5);
- line 7 (else): A[i][j] := A[i][j+1]; j := j+1.

The printed line 3 compares with A[i][j]; it must compare the two neighbours, A[i][j+1].

steps.title: Place x (line 9) and cost
steps.body: When neither neighbour is smaller, A[i][j] := x. Each pass increases i or j, so at most $2n-2$ passes: $O(n)$. The guarantee that x is smaller than the last row/column keeps i, j < n inside the loop.

pitfalls: Moving the larger neighbour breaks the order with the other neighbour.
Line 9 writes x, not a neighbour.

cse-1996-b-64.approach: Use the cut property: an edge that is the unique lightest edge across some cut is in every MST. For |u−v| the weight-1 edges already form a spanning tree; for u+v, edge (0, v) is the lightest edge at every vertex v.

steps.title: (a) weight |u − v|
steps.body: Every edge weighs at least 1, and the $n-1$ edges of weight 1 are $(0,1),(1,2),\ldots,(n-2,n-1)$, which form a path through all vertices. A spanning tree has $n-1$ edges, so weight $\ge n-1$; the path achieves it. MST = **path** $0-1-2-\cdots-(n-1)$, weight $n-1$.

steps.title: (b) weight u + v
steps.body: For a vertex $v\ge1$, its edges weigh $v+u$; the lightest is $(0,v)$ with weight $v$ (unique). By the cut property on the cut $\{v\}$ vs. the rest, $(0,v)$ is in every MST. These $n-1$ edges already form a spanning tree: the **star** centred at 0.

answer.value: (a) The path $0-1-2-\cdots-(n-1)$ (weight $n-1$). (b) The star with centre 0: edges $(0,v)$ for $v=1,\ldots,n-1$ (weight $n(n-1)/2$).

pitfalls: In (b) a path 0–1–2–… costs $1+3+5+\cdots$, more than the star.
cse-1996-b-64.verification: n = 4, (b): star 1 + 2 + 3 = 6; any tree must contain each edge (0, v) by the cut argument, so 6 is optimal.

cse-1996-b-66.approach: Look for a range where the loop makes no progress. Because the update is i := k (not k+1) and k = (i+j) div 2, a two-element range j = i+1 gives k = i, and if a[i] < x then i stays i forever.

steps.title: Find the stuck state
steps.body: If $j=i+1$ then $k=\lfloor(2i+1)/2\rfloor=i$. If $a[i]<x$: i := k = i, nothing changes, $a[k]\ne x$ and $i<j$, so the **loop never ends**. (If $a[i]\ge x$, j := i and the loop stops.)

steps.title: When is that state reached?
steps.body: The updates keep the invariant "if x is present it is in a[i..j]" and, once $a[1]<x$, also $a[i]<x$. So if $x>a[1]$ and x is never hit exactly at a probe k, the range shrinks to $j=i+1$ with $a[i]<x$ and the program hangs.

steps.title: Failing cases
When it works
steps.body: If $x\le a[1]$ the search moves j down to 1 and stops with the right message; if x is hit at some probe it stops with "x is in the array". It never prints a wrong message — the only failure is non-termination.

answer.value: The program loops forever whenever the range shrinks to $j=i+1$ with $a[i]<x$ (then $k=i$ and i := k makes no progress). This happens whenever $x>a[1]$ and x is not hit at a probe — i.e. x is absent and greater than $a[1]$, or x = a[N] (> a[1]); e.g. a = (1, 2), x = 2. Fix: use i := k+1.

pitfalls: The program never gives a wrong answer; it fails by not terminating.
cse-1996-b-66.verification: a = (1, 2, 3, 4): x = 3 is found at the second probe; x = 4 gets stuck at i = 3, j = 4, matching the rule.

answer.value: (i) point 1: 5 5; point 2: 10 10; point3: 10. (ii) point 1: 5 3; point 2: 5 10; point3: 5.

cse-1996-b-68.approach: An LR parser reduces bottom-up and left to right, so the print actions fire in post-order of the parse tree: each operand is printed before the operator that combines them — a postfix translation.

steps.title: Parse tree
steps.body: Root $E\to E*E$. Left child $E\to(E)$ with inside $E\to E+E$ over $E\to id(a)$, $E\to id(b)$; right child $E\to(E)$ with inside $E\to E+E$ over $id(c)$, $id(d)$.

steps.title: Reductions in order
steps.body:
1. $a\to E$: print **a**
2. $b\to E$: print **b**
3. $E+E\to E$: print **+**
4. $(E)\to E$: nothing
5. $c\to E$: **c**; 6. $d\to E$: **d**; 7. $E+E$: **+**; 8. $(E)$: nothing
9. $E*E\to E$: print \*

answer.value: Translation: a b + c d + * (postfix of (a+b)*(c+d)).

pitfalls: The rule $E\to(E)$ has no action, so parentheses never appear in the output.

cse-1996-b-69.approach: Trace which process reaches each join first: join N (N = 2) lets through only the second of the two arrivals (S1's and S2's processes), and join M (M = 2) only the second of S3's and S4's.

steps.title: Processes created
steps.body: fork L3 starts a process running S2 then goto L1; fork L4 starts one running S4 then goto L2. The parent runs S1 and falls into L1. So S1, S2, S4 run concurrently.

steps.body: The parent (after S1) and the L3 process (after S2) both reach join N. The first decrements N to 1 and terminates; the second gets 0 and continues to S3. So **S1 → S3** and **S2 → S3**.

steps.title: join M at L2
steps.body: The process from S3 and the L4 process (after S4) meet at join M; the survivor runs S5. So **S3 → S5** and **S4 → S5**.

cse-1996-b-70.approach: Compute Need = Max − Allocation and run the safety algorithm. For the request, pretend to grant it and run the safety check again.

steps.title: (a) Safety check
steps.body:
Work = (2, 2, 0).
- P1: Need (1, 2, 0) ≤ (2, 2, 0) ✓ → Work = (2, 2, 0) + (0, 3, 1) = (2, 5, 1).
- P0: Need (3, 1, 0) — 3 > 2 ✗; P2: Need (0, 2, 1) ≤ (2, 5, 1) ✓ → Work = (3, 5, 3).
- P0: (3, 1, 0) ≤ (3, 5, 3) ✓ → Work = (4, 5, 5).

Safe sequence **P1, P2, P0**, so the state is safe and the system can be in it (totals (4, 5, 5) cover every Max).

steps.title: (b) Pretend to grant (0, 1, 0) to P0
steps.body: Request ≤ Need (0,1,0) ≤ (3,1,0) ✓ and ≤ Available ✓. New Available = (2, 1, 0); P0 Allocation (1, 1, 2); P0 Need (3, 0, 0).

steps.title: (b) Safety check fails
steps.body: Work = (2, 1, 0): P0 needs 3 of R0 (> 2), P1 needs 2 of R1 (> 1), P2 needs 2 of R1 and 1 of R2 (> 1, > 0). No process can finish → **unsafe**. The request is not granted; P0 waits and the state is rolled back.

answer.value: (a) The state is safe: P1, P2, P0 can finish in that order. (b) Granting would leave the system unsafe, so the request is denied and P0 waits.

pitfalls: A request that fits in Available can still be refused — the test is safety, not availability.
cse-1996-b-70.verification: Total resources = Allocation sums + Available = (4, 5, 5) ≥ each process's Max.

cse-1996-b-71.approach: The number of files is limited by how many 32-bit directory entries fit in one 4 KB block; the file size is limited by how many data blocks an 8-bit FAT pointer can name.

steps.title: (a) Maximum number of files
steps.body: Directory = one block of $4\text{ KB}=4096$ bytes; entry = 32 bits = 4 bytes. $4096/4=1024$ entries → **1024 files**.

steps.title: (b) Maximum file size
steps.body: A FAT entry is 8 bits, so it can name at most $2^8=256$ different data blocks. (The 4 KB FAT block has room for 4096 entries, but only 256 blocks are addressable.) A single file can use at most all of them: **256 blocks** ($256\times4\text{ KB}=1\text{ MB}$).

steps.title: Remark
steps.body: If one 8-bit value is reserved as the end-of-chain / free marker, only 255 data blocks can be named, giving 255 blocks.

answer.value: (a) 1024 files; (b) 256 blocks (255 if one FAT value is reserved as the end-of-file marker).

pitfalls: The FAT block could hold 4096 one-byte entries, but 8-bit pointers limit the disk to 256 data blocks.

cse-1996-b-75.approach: Use the hierarchical model: every access pays level 1; a level-1 miss also pays level 2; a level-2 miss also pays level 3. $T=t_1+(1-h_1)\,[\,t_2+(1-h_2)\,t_3\,]$. Try the smallest level-1 size first.

steps.title: Choice
steps.body: The smallest (most expensive) cache, 8M, works only with the 64M main memory. So level 1 = **8M bytes**, level 2 = **64M bytes**, average **95 ns**.

steps.title: Caveat
steps.body: 16M cache with 4M main memory gives $50+0.1\times300=80$ ns with less total memory, and a model where each level's time is counted alone ($h_1t_1+(1-h_1)h_2t_2+\ldots$) makes 8M + 4M already reach 99.2 ns. The intended reading of "minimum sizes" is therefore uncertain.

answer.value: (a) Level 1 = 8M bytes, Level 2 = 64M bytes; (b) 95 ns (hierarchical model).

pitfalls: 16M main memory gives exactly 100 ns, which is not less than 100 ns.

answer.value: (a) The titles of all books issued to the user whose User# is 6. (b) The names of authors whose books have been issued to users whose home town is Delhi.

pitfalls: In (a) the selection after projection still works because User# is kept by the projection.
cse-1996-b-76.verification: Both queries only use attributes kept by their inner operations (User# in (a), AuthorName in (b)).
